LLM memory in the strict sense is what the model absorbed during training. It's compressed patterns, not a lookup table, which is why a model can confidently repeat something outdated. Fine-tuning can add domain knowledge, but it's slow, expensive, hard to inspect, and it can't capture anything from a live session.

Context engineering is choosing what goes into the context window for this particular call. Bigger windows help, but they don't solve memory: the context vanishes when the session ends, long prompts cost more, and models don't attend equally to everything in a very long input.

RAG retrieves from an existing knowledge source (docs, a database, an API) and adds the results to the prompt. The key limitation is direction: RAG reads, but it doesn't write back. It won't remember what the user asked last week or which fix already failed.

Agent memory starts where the agent writes back. It captures new facts, preferences and outcomes as it works, and retrieves them later. Picture a sales assistant that pulls this quarter's numbers via RAG, but also remembers from earlier conversations that this user wants EU figures in euros, broken down by country. 

How agent memory actually works

At a high level, any memory system needs three pieces: a data store where memories are persisted, write logic that decides what gets stored and how,  and a retrieval interface that lets the agent find the relevant memories. The store you choose has a big influence on the other two: which write logic makes sense, and what retrieval can do. So here are the main architectures, by store type.

Vector databases. Memories are turned into embeddings and found by semantic similarity. Easy to set up and well supported, but similarity isn't everything. "Q3 sales" and "Q4 sales" sit almost on top of each other in vector space, there's no notion of which fact is current, and an entry that's relevant but phrased differently can be missed entirely.

Plain files. The agent keeps a MEMORY.md (or similar) that it reads and edits. Coding agents popularized this. It's transparent and version-controlled, but retrieval is limited to loading everything or grep-ping, and sharing a file between many agents gets messy fast.

Knowledge graphs. Facts become entities and relationships: the sales report covers EU deals, EU deals are booked in euros, the figures come from the billing export. Retrieval finds an entry point, then follows the edges, so the agent gets facts that are logically related to the question, not only ones that sound similar. The trade-off is more work at ingestion time.

Hybrid systems. In practice, no single store covers everything. Exact IDs want a structured index, relationships want a graph, fuzzy matching wants vectors, and "what did the customer prefer last March?" needs timestamps. Production memory layers combine stores and put logic on top that decides what goes where. This is also why a memory layer is more than a database: the stores are just where the data lives, and the memory layer sits on top of them. It decides what gets stored and in what form, and exposes the operations agents use to write, retrieve, update and forget.

Architecture

Retrieval

Strength

Watch out for

Semantic similarity

Simple, scalable, mature tooling

No entities, weak on exact IDs, no recency

Load all or search text

Transparent, versioned, no infra

Doesn't scale or share well

Hybrid

Covers mixed data: exact IDs, relationships, fuzzy matches and time-aware queries

Needs more components to set up and run

Memory has to be managed, not just accumulated

A memory layer that only grows gets worse over time. Facts change, preferences shift, and stale entries start competing with correct ones. Good memory systems handle several processes on top of storage. The main three are:

  • Consolidation. Raw entries pile up faster than they become useful. The system should periodically turn them into fewer, higher-level records (summaries, derived facts) while keeping a trail back to the originals.
  • Updating. When a fact changes, a blind overwrite loses history: what was true before, and when it changed. Keeping time information on facts lets the agent answer both "what's true now?" and "what did we believe in March?"
  • Forgetting. Some data has to go: a stale dataset, a correction, a deletion request. That should be an explicit, deliberate operation, separate from the softer job of letting less useful memories fade in relevance.

The best systems also learn from use. If an answer gets confirmed, the memories behind it gain weight; if it gets corrected, the misleading ones drop. Over weeks, retrieval should get sharper, not noisier.

How do you know your memory works?

Public benchmarks give a useful first signal. Most follow the same two-phase pattern: feed a long history into the memory system, then ask questions whose answers depend on storing and retrieving the right facts, including ones that were later updated or contradicted.

Size matters more than people expect. If a benchmark's whole history fits in a modern context window, you can skip memory entirely and paste everything into the prompt, so the test says more about the model than about the memory. That doesn't mean the model will answer perfectly, though: models don't use long contexts evenly, and details buried in the middle of a long prompt can get less attention. LoCoMo conversations run around 26k tokens; LongMemEval's common variant is about 115k. BEAM is the most demanding of the three, testing ten memory abilities over conversations of up to 10M tokens, which is where external memory actually has to do the work. The reported state of the art on BEAM is 79% at 100K tokens and 67% at 10M, set by Cognee, up from the previous best of 73.4% and 64.1%.

But benchmarks mostly check final answers. They don't look at what the memory actually stored, how it holds up after weeks of updates, or how it behaves when many agents share it. For a full map of what each benchmark measures and where it falls short, see this guide to AI memory benchmarks.

The test that matters most is your own: run the same workflow with memory on and off, and measure the outcome you care about, such as tickets resolved, fewer repeated questions, or correct follow-ups.

Adding n8n workflows memory

n8n workflows share a trait with LLMs: by default, each execution starts fresh. So a support workflow that drafted a fix on Monday won't automatically know about it when a follow-up arrives on Wednesday. Many teams handle this with a Postgres table or an Airtable base, which works, but each workflow then needs its own storage setup and its own rules for what to keep.

1. A shared brain for all your workflows

At its simplest, memory lets any workflow pick up where the last run left off. One node stores what the workflow learned; another looks it up on the next run. And because the memory lives outside any single workflow, many workflows can share it.

The biggest payoff is a centralized "brain": one shared memory that all your workflows write to and read from. Extend it to the whole company and you get a "company brain". Most useful context already exists across the company: Slack threads, tickets, docs, CRM notes, call transcripts. n8n can collect it from all those tools, and a memory layer can structure and connect it, so every workflow draws on the same picture of what the company knows.

The pattern is simple:

  • Collector workflows use n8n's triggers and app integrations to pick up new material as it appears, such as a closed ticket, a call summary or a form submission, and send it to the memory layer, which structures and connects it.
  • Acting workflows query that same memory right before they do something: draft a reply, route an escalation, prep a sales brief. They can ask in plain English, like "What's the current status with Acme, and what did we promise them?", and pass the answer on to the next node.

Because both sides point at the same memory, workflows share context without sharing implementation details. And when the memory keeps relationships between entities, acting workflows get connected answers, such as which contracts expire next quarter or which accounts share the same root cause, that a pure similarity search would miss.

2. Memory inside an agentic workflow

The second pattern lives inside a single n8n AI Agent, and it maps onto the short-term and long-term split from earlier. Without memory, every message the agent receives starts from zero. n8n handles the short-term side through the AI Agent's Memory port. n8n's default, "Simple Memory", stores a customizable length of chat history for the current session, and it's the easiest way to get started. You can stick with this default or choose a more advanced third-party memory provider, as shown below: 

Chat memory, though, only remembers the conversation. Long-term knowledge, such as user preferences, the outcomes of past tasks and company context, needs more than a chat log. For that, connect a memory layer to the Agent's Tool port, where you attach add-ons the agent can use to access extra context or resources. The agent can then decide for itself when to remember something new and when to search what the company already knows. The result is an agent that holds the thread of the current conversation and can reach into shared company knowledge mid-task.

In short: n8n's built-in memory is a good starting point for a single chat agent. But if you want memory that evolves over time and is shared across workflows and agents, combine it with a memory layer: chat memory for the conversation at hand, and shared memory so every run starts from what the company already knows rather than from zero.

Conclusion

LLMs start every call from zero, so building AI agents that work reliably over time requires memory outside the model. But storing information is only half the challenge. Agents also need a way to capture, retrieve, and act on the right context across tasks and workflows.

n8n and Cognee solve these challenges together. n8n connects your apps, orchestrates AI agents, and automates how information flows between systems. Cognee turns that information into structured, persistent memory that agents can retrieve, update, and share.

Together, they let you build AI workflows that don't just execute tasks independently, but learn from previous interactions, maintain context across sessions, and work from a shared understanding of your company's knowledge.

Ready to build AI agents with long-term memory? Get started with n8n and connect Cognee to give your workflows a shared memory layer.

item.title: Hallucination detection methods for AI agent workflows
item.description: Learn practical hallucination detection methods for AI workflows. See how your team can identify unreliable outputs before they spread.
item.dc:creator: n8n team
item.content:encoded:
AI agent hallucinations are hard to catch because they usually look like normal answers. An agent can invent a fact, misread retrieved context, or contradict itself without signaling that anything went wrong. Once that output triggers another workflow step, the mistake can quickly become a production problem.

Effective hallucination detection methods don’t rely on a single score. They need to be as multi-faceted as the hallucinations they catch. In this guide, we’ll break down how those methods work, where each one falls short, and how to layer them into AI workflows that are easier to inspect and control.

Types of AI hallucinations

Not all AI hallucinations fail in the same way. Models might invent a fact, drift away from the context they’ve been given, fill a knowledge gap with plausible-sounding details, or contradict something they said earlier.

Knowing which failure you’re dealing with matters because each type calls for a different detection method. Here are the four main types of hallucinations to watch for:

  • Factual hallucinations: The model makes a claim that conflicts with verifiable facts, like inventing a statistic, person, or event.
  • Contextual hallucinations: The answer isn’t supported by the context supplied to the model. This is especially important in RAG systems, where an answer can sound reasonable while misrepresenting or going beyond the retrieved material.
  • Confabulations: The model fills gaps with details that weren’t provided or established, producing a coherent answer without sufficient evidence.
  • Self-contradictions: The model produces claims that conflict with other parts of its own response or with information it provided earlier.

These distinctions show why there’s no universal hallucination detector. A groundedness check can identify claims that stray from retrieved context, for example, but it won’t necessarily tell you whether the source material itself is factually correct. In production systems, reliable detection means matching the check to the failure mode — and often layering several checks together.

Detection methods that work in production

LLM hallucination detection works best as a layered system. No single check catches every failure mode: Some methods compare an answer with its context, others look for inconsistent outputs or uncertainty, and others escalate questionable results to a person. Combining these signals gives you more coverage than treating one score as a definitive pass or fail.

Faithfulness and groundedness checks

Faithfulness checks ask whether the model’s claims are actually supported by the context it received. For example, in a RAG workflow, you can break an answer into individual claims and compare each one with the retrieved documents, producing a score based on how much of the response can be traced back to that context. 

Tools like DeepEval can automate this process, making faithfulness scoring useful for automated hallucination detection across test sets, evaluation datasets, and live outputs.

Self-consistency checks

With self-consistency checks, you ask the model the same question multiple times, then compare the answers. If independently generated responses converge on the same claims, you’ve got a useful consistency signal; if they disagree substantially, the output deserves more scrutiny. Because this method compares the model against its own outputs, it doesn’t require an external knowledge base. 

The limitation is important, though: Different inference runs can converge on the same incorrect information. So think of consistency as a signal, not proof of accuracy.

Semantic entropy and uncertainty estimation

Semantic entropy looks beyond whether generated answers use the same words and asks whether they express the same underlying meaning. Generate several responses to the same prompt, group semantically equivalent answers, then estimate how probability is distributed across those meaning clusters. 

High semantic entropy indicates that the model is uncertain about what the answer should be, making it useful for identifying outputs that need another validation step. Like self-consistency, however, uncertainty estimation tells you how stable an answer is, not whether it’s factually correct.

See n8n's AI agent architecture in action.

Explore the template library

Source and retrieval verification

Faithfulness asks whether an answer reflects the context the model received; source verification asks whether its claims hold up against an authoritative external source. That distinction matters for a RAG hallucination caused by poor retrieval: A perfectly faithful answer can still be wrong if the retrieved document is outdated, irrelevant, or incorrect. Production workflows can verify important claims against authoritative repositories like databases, APIs, and documentation, making this approach especially useful when there’s a clear source of truth.

Confidence thresholds and human in the loop

Not every questionable output needs the same response. You can define confidence thresholds that route high-confidence results forward automatically, send ambiguous outputs through additional checks, and hold high-risk cases for a human in the loop before an agent takes an external action. The threshold should reflect the consequences of getting something wrong: An internal summary can tolerate more uncertainty than an agent preparing to modify a customer record or trigger a business process. This tiered approach lets teams keep humans in control where judgment matters without requiring manual approval for every execution.

💡
In addition to Human-in-the-loop, there’s also a Human-on-the-loop approach to control LLM output quality after the workflow execution.

Implementing detection with open-source tools

In practice, hallucination detection usually means combining an LLM evaluation framework with workflow logic that decides what happens when a check fails. A code-first framework like DeepEval can calculate metrics like faithfulness scoring, while guardrail libraries can add validation around model outputs. 

In n8n, a source-available AI-native automation platform, you can add checks around LLMs on the visual canvas and use the results to decide whether an output continues or gets retried or routed elsewhere. This keeps evaluation logic inside the same workflow that produced the answer instead of splitting detection across separate systems.

That workflow context also matters for AI agent observability. The AI Agent node keeps model and tool activity within an inspectable execution path, letting teams trace what the agent received and what it generated. 

If a workflow fails, an Error Trigger node can start a separate error-handling workflow, while execution history lets you debug executions using the data from a previous run. The result is a layered setup: Evaluations and guardrails measure the model output, and workflow logic acts on the confidence score and routes the output to a corresponding branch. Finally, execution records give you the context to investigate failures.

Why detection alone isn’t enough

Hallucination detection reduces risk, but it can’t guarantee that every incorrect output gets caught. Scores depend on the quality of the context and evaluation method, thresholds can produce false positives or miss subtle errors, and even a well-grounded response can be wrong if its source is unreliable. 

Detection works best alongside prevention, clear escalation paths, and LLM observability. When something does slip through, visibility into the model’s inputs, retrieved context, outputs, and downstream actions helps you trace the failure and improve the workflow instead of just flagging the results.

Building hallucination checks into production workflows

In production, each detection method covers a different failure mode, so the strongest workflows layer several checks: 

  • Faithfulness checks test whether claims match the supplied context.
  • Source verification checks them against authoritative information.
  • Consistency or uncertainty measures help identify answers that deserve more scrutiny.
  • For higher-risk decisions, confidence thresholds can route an output to human review.

The important part is what happens after a problem is detected. In production, a flagged response needs somewhere to go: another validation step, a retry, an error workflow, or a person who can make the final call. Building those paths into the workflow makes hallucination detection part of how the AI system operates, not a test you run after something’s already gone wrong.

Tired of building observability from scratch?

See how n8n's execution history works.

Learn more

Put hallucination detection into practice with n8n

n8n gives you one place to orchestrate those safeguards alongside your AI agents to improve AI agent reliability. You can add custom evaluation logic, route flagged responses for approval, inspect execution data, and define what happens next when a check fails.

Ready to weave detection methods into production? Get started with n8n Cloud, or self-host the free Community Edition for full control over your AI workflows.

FAQ

How do I make sure my AI agent isn’t hallucinating?

You can’t completely prevent AI hallucinations, but you can catch more unreliable outputs by layering checks. Test responses for faithfulness, verify important claims against trusted sources, flag uncertain answers, and require human review when the risk of an incorrect action is high.

Do hallucination detection tools support multimodal outputs like images and audio?

Some do, but support depends on the detection tool and model. Multimodal evaluation can check outputs like images and audio, while text-only methods may require you to first extract a transcript or description.

Can hallucination detection block a bad answer before the user sees it?

Yes, run detection before the response reaches the user, then use a threshold to determine what happens next. A flagged output can be stopped, regenerated, sent through another validation check, or held for human approval instead of being returned automatically.

item.title: API versioning strategies for stable workflow integrations
item.description: Compare API versioning strategies like URI, header, and date-based approaches, and learn how to handle a provider’s deprecation without breaking integration
item.dc:creator: Yulia Dmitrievna
item.content:encoded:
An API integration can work perfectly for months. Then the provider decides to improve its endpoints, change response formats, and retire old version behavior. If a breaking change reaches production before your workflow is ready, downstream steps may receive the wrong data before anyone notices.

API versioning reduces that risk by separating incompatible changes from the version your integration already uses. By keeping older behavior available while introducing a new version, providers let you update, test, and migrate integrations on your own schedule.

What is API versioning?

API versioning is the practice of maintaining distinct versions of an application programming interface (API) so providers can change how it works on their end without forcing every existing integration to update the moment those changes are released.

Each version represents a familiar interface that your workflow expects, including when API endpoints are available, the data they accept or return, and how requests and responses behave.

When you rely on a third-party API, the provider decides when new versions and API breaking changes are released. Pinning your integration to a specific version gives you time to review those changes and migrate at your own pace.

The same principle applies to REST API versioning. Providers can keep different interfaces available so they don't force new behavior on existing integrations. If a change is backward compatible, existing integrations can usually keep working without modification. Versioning comes into play when a change breaks that backward compatibility.

Common API versioning strategies

You’ll usually see an API versioned in the following ways:

  • The URL path; e.g., `/v1/products `
  • An HTTP header; e.g., `curl -H “Accepts-version: 1.0” http://www.example.com/api/products` 
  • As a date; e.g., `/2026.10/` as part of an API endpoint
  • A query parameter; e.g., `example-api.com/products?version=v1`

The provider’s API design decides which approach to use, so your job is to understand where the version is and what it means for your integration. The design can affect how clearly caches distinguish between responses or how easily you can spot the active version while debugging.

Here are the four API versioning strategies in more detail.

1. URI versioning

With URI versioning, or URL path versioning, the version appears directly in the API’s URL. One version might have a URL structure containing v1, while the newer version uses v2.

The active version is easy to see in your workflow, logs, and API documentation. If an API request fails or returns data in a format your workflow doesn’t expect, you can check the URL immediately to confirm which version your integration used. You don’t need to look elsewhere in the request for that information. Since each version has its own URL, caching systems can also tell them apart easily.

2. Header versioning

In this type of versioning, the API URL stays the same, and your workflow sends the version in an HTTP header instead. A header is extra information attached to a request, such as authentication details or data type, and can tell the provider which API version you want to use.

URLs stay consistent even when the provider releases new versions. However, the version becomes less visible, so if an API starts returning unexpected data, looking at the URL won’t tell you which version handled the request. You need to check the header versioning versus the URI versioning.

Caching systems also need to account for the version header — two requests can use the same URL but ask for different versions.

3. Date-based versioning

With date-based versioning, the provider identifies a version by its release date instead of a version number like v1 or v2. This is different from semantic versioning for an API, where the provider uses a version number like 2.1.0 to distinguish major, minor, and patch releases.

If your workflow uses a version from a specific date, you can compare it with the provider’s release notes to see how the changes in later versions affect your integration.

However, the date itself doesn’t explain those changes. You have to review the provider’s documentation and test the newer version before switching. Some providers send the date through an HTTP header, so you can combine data-based versioning with header versioning.

4. Query parameter

In query parameter versioning, the version appears as an extra setting at the end of the API URL. The main part of the URL stays the same, while the added parameter tells the provider which version should handle the request.

The version remains visible when you inspect the request. You can see what resource the workflow asked for and which API version it asked to use without checking a separate header. That makes it handy for troubleshooting and confirming whether the workflow still points to the intended version.

A caching system, however, may see two URLs that differ only by their version parameter, even though each returns different data. If the caching system ignores the parameter, it could serve a response from the wrong version. When that happens, it’s best to set the version parameter for your integration and make sure the systems handling those requests can tell them apart.

What to watch for when a provider deprecates a version

Your API deprecation strategy should include monitoring headers and other metadata for signals that an API version is scheduled for retirement. A deprecation header is usually the first sign and tells you that the version is or will be deprecated. You should flag the integration for migration before it stops working, even if the API still works normally.

A sunset header adds an exact end date for when the version is expected to become unavailable. You can use the remaining time to test and switch versions. After that point, the provider may return 410 Gone, which means the requested resource is no longer available and the condition is likely permanent. Don’t retry the same version or send the same request. Instead, your workflow should detect the response and route it for handling.

Build version migration into your workflow before the provider forces it on you

Version migration is easier to manage when your workflow is purpose-built to expect API changes. n8n is a source-available, AI-native automation platform where engineering teams can create AI agents and agentic workflows that anticipate API versioning.

In n8n, built-in nodes handle API versioning for you. If a node is not available, you can use the HTTP Request node to connect a workflow to a third-party API and make the API version part of the workflow’s configuration. Instead of relying on whatever version the provider uses by default, you can specify the version yourself in the request URL, header, or parameter. That means the workflow keeps asking for the version you built and tested it against and won’t unexpectedly inherit different behavior when the provider changes its default.

You can also make the workflow respond differently when that version starts reaching the end of its life. Try inspecting the response status and headers and check for a deprecation warning or a 410 Gone response. A warning can trigger an alert or other workflow that gives you time to schedule a migration.

If the version is already gone, you can stop the normal path and send the failure to a separate error workflow, where an Error Trigger node can start a recovery process. If the recovery process needs custom parsing, you can add custom Code in n8n to normalize or validate it before deciding what happens next.

If the API provider explicitly specifies the deprecation date, you can add an IF node and route API requests based on the current server date.

n8n also maintains execution history so you can return to previous runs when troubleshooting. You can debug executions by loading data from a failed production execution back into the current workflow, checking what happened, making a change, and testing it again against the previous execution data. This feature is available on multiple editions, including all n8n Cloud plans and Registered Community, Business, and Enterprise editions for self-hosted n8n.

In n8n, you can build API integrations that are ready for version changes and give them a safer migration path.

Prepare for the API version changes you don’t control with n8n

API versioning becomes easier to manage when you separate what the provider controls from what you control. You can’t choose whether an API uses a URL, header, date, or query parameter, but you can decide whether your integration depends on the provider’s default or handles that version proactively.

In n8n, you can keep version-handling logic visible with the rest of the workflow. Prepare inside the workflow and watch the API request and its failure paths to make the best possible decision for migration and managing changes. 

Try n8n Cloud for a hosted setup, or explore self-hosting in n8n if you prefer managing your own environment.

item.title: Stateful vs. stateless: Managing context in AI agent builds
item.description: Stateful versus stateless design changes how systems scale and remember context. Learn when to use memory nodes, state stores, or both.
item.dc:creator: n8n team
item.content:encoded:
State is the information an AI agent carries across tasks and, from conversation history to long-term memory and user profiles. Choosing between stateful versus stateless architecture shapes how agentic workflows manage scale and recover from failures. It’s a core design decision with implications for your entire system’s reliability and performance.

Stateful vs. stateless: The core concepts

The difference between stateful and stateless architecture comes down to what happens to information between interactions. Does the system retain what happened from earlier interactions, or does it start every request with a blank slate?

Before comparing stateful versus stateless applications, it helps to define three related terms:

  • State: Information that persists beyond a single interaction, such as a shopping cart, authentication status, or conversation history.
  • Session: A series of related interactions associated with the same user or process. It gives the system a boundary for deciding which interactions belong together.
  • Context: The information the LLM-powered system uses to understand and respond to the current request. It can come from the current input, previous interactions, or stored data.

Stateful applications

A stateful application retains information from previous interactions and uses it to handle future ones. That information might include conversation history, authentication details, shopping cart contents, or progress through a multi-step process.

The advantage of statefulness is continuity. The application can pick up where an earlier interaction left off. The trade-off is that you need somewhere to store and manage that state and ensure it's available when the next request arrives.

Stateless applications

A stateless application treats each request independently. This means everything needed to process the request must arrive alongside it or be retrieved from another system. There’s no falling back on information retained from the previous request.

It’s easier to distribute requests across instances in stateless applications. Any suitable instance can handle the request because it doesn’t need to recover state elsewhere. This can make the application more scalable and fault-tolerant. But when continuity matters, you need to introduce state somewhere in the system. That's why many architectures use a stateless request-processing layer while storing persistent data in a cache or other shared system.

💡
Modern LLM apps also have a scratchpad. This is a temporary storage where an AI agent keeps its intermediary results before responding to the user. The scratchpad is not part of a stateful system and serves primarily to store information while the agent sends multiple queries to the LLM during a single user request.

Key differences between stateful and stateless

The practical differences in stateful versus stateless architecture start with where information lives. In a stateful system, the application retains information between requests. In a stateless system, each request contains or retrieves what it needs independently. That decision affects how the system scales, recovers from failures, and uses resources.

Stateful Stateless
State retention Retains information across requests or sessions Processes each request independently
Scalability State must remain accessible as traffic moves between instances Requests can be distributed more freely across available instances
Fault tolerance A server crash can disrupt access to state unless it's replicated or persisted elsewhere Another server can typically process the next request without recovering local session state
Complexity and resources Requires infrastructure for storing, synchronizing, and recovering state Simpler application instances, but persistent data may need external state storage

You don’t need to make an entire system stateful or stateless. Many architectures keep compute stateless for easier scaling while moving the state that needs to persist into a database, cache, or other shared store.

Are AI agents and LLMs stateful or stateless?

LLMs don’t automatically retain the conversation from one inference request to the next. If an application wants a model to use previous messages, they must be supplied in the model’s input or retrieved elsewhere in the system.

AI agents can behave statefully by giving the model access to information from earlier interactions. That’s how memory works — the agent stores and retrieves state outside the model, then adds relevant context to future requests.

How that state is stored depends on how long it needs to last and who needs access to it. An in-memory buffer can hold recent messages within a session, while a persistent store can preserve them beyond a single process or restart. In distributed systems, a shared store can make state available across multiple points.

When to use stateful vs. stateless APIs 

Use stateless APIs for scale and simplicity. REST APIs are a good example. Each request contains the info necessary to authenticate and process it. Remember that stateless requests can be easily distributed across multiple instances. This is especially helpful if you need an API to grow its capacity without slowing down or crashing.

Use stateful APIs when context must persist. Stateful behavior makes sense for conversations, multi-step processes, and other interactions where the next step depends on what happened before. This architecture is especially useful for session-cookie authentication APIs, FTP APIs, and real-time APIs for activities like chat or gaming.

Agent state in n8n: Memory nodes vs. state stores

n8n is a source-available, AI-native automation platform where engineering teams can build AI agents and agentic workflows. In n8n, you can choose where state lives based on what needs to persist. An AI Agent node can use Memory nodes for conversational context, while state stores hold data that needs to survive beyond an agent session. This lets you add state where it’s useful without making the entire workflow stateful.

Stateless by default

n8n workflow executions are independent. One execution doesn’t automatically remember data from the previous one, which keeps the execution layer simpler to scale and recover. When a workflow needs continuity, you explicitly add the appropriate form of state.

Execution history also gives you visibility into the data that moved through each run, making stateful behavior easier to inspect and debug.

Short-term/session state with Memory nodes

Memory nodes give AI agents access to previous messages within a session. The Simple Memory node provides an in-memory buffer for recent conversation history, but it’s not compatible with queue mode.

When memory needs to persist beyond the running process, the Postgres Chat Memory node uses a persistent store and separates conversations by session ID. Redis Chat Memory offers another option when you need a fast distributed cache that can share session state across workers. For distributed execution in queue mode, use a persistent memory option so session state remains available across workers. And when you need more control over conversation history, Chat Memory Manager lets workflows load, insert, and clear messages explicitly.

These approaches to AI Agent Memory let you match storage to the lifespan and scale of the conversation. For example, an AI agent chat can use session memory to keep earlier messages available as the conversation continues.

💡
Most modern LLMs have a caching mechanism that significantly reduces costs. If you use a memory node with a sliding window (i.e. the last 20 messages), it invalidates the cache during long conversations. We recommend either increasing the size of the sliding window or implementing a more advanced technique (i.e. summarizing the last X messages instead of using a naïve sliding window).

Durable, shared state with state stores

Some state needs to outlive a conversation or remain available across workflow executions. n8n data tables provide persistent, structured storage that workflows can read from and write to across executions. Depending on the use case, you can also use workflow static data or an external Postgres or Redis store.

Using Memory nodes alongside state stores gives you two distinct layers of state. Chat memory nodes preserve conversational context for an agent, while state stores persist workflow and application data across executions in a data table or an SQL database.

Build stateless, then add state where you need it

Stateful versus stateless doesn’t have to be a system-wide choice. Start with independent, stateless execution where possible, then introduce state wherever your workflow needs continuity.

For AI agents in n8n, that might mean adding session memory for an ongoing conversation, persistent memory when context needs to survive restarts, or a shared state store when data needs to carry across workflows and executions. Choosing the right layer keeps state deliberate instead of letting it become an architectural constraint.

Build stateful behavior on a stateless foundation you control. Start for free or explore n8n's templates.

item.title: Self-hosted LLM vs. cloud APIs: How to route between them
item.description: A self-hosted LLM isn’t always cheaper than an API. Learn when on-prem wins, what your hardware can run, and how to route between local and cloud models.
item.dc:creator: n8n team
item.content:encoded:
A self-hosted LLM can give you more control over where your data lives. If the model and the workflow handling its requests both run on infrastructure you control, prompts can stay inside your network instead of passing through an external provider.

Self-hosting can be appealing for sensitive workloads. But it also requires hardware, maintenance, and operational overhead that cloud-based APIs mostly offload. 

A hybrid option offers a way to route requests locally or to the cloud without managing two disconnected systems.

The best self-hosting LLM open-weight models

An open-weight model makes its trained model weights available for you to download and run on your own infrastructure.

Look at the tasks you want the model to do, try open-weight models via OpenRouter or another provider first. Once you have found the smallest model that handles your task reliably, you can deploy it on your infrastructure. A smaller model usually needs less compute and responds faster, so moving up in size makes sense when the extra capability measurably improves results for your workflow.

Params, short for parameters, measure a model’s size. For example, a 24B model has around 24 billion learned parameters. Larger models can be more capable, but they also need more compute and memory.

Min VRAM is the approximate minimum amount of GPU memory needed to run the model. If the model doesn’t fit into your available VRAM, you need a smaller model, or a quantized version of the model, or stronger hardware to support it.

Here are a few open-weight models for self-hosting, with their parameters and minimum recommended VRAM.

Scroll for more →
Model Params Min VRAM* Best for
Phi-4-mini 3.8B ~8 GB A lightweight starting point for local assistants and tasks when you have limited hardware
Qwen3 8B 8B ~8 GB (8-bit configuration) General-purpose option for chat, coding, and multilingual workloads that doesn't require high-end GPU hardware
Gemma 3 12B 12B ~12–16 GB (when quantized) General reasoning, summarization, and multimodal tasks like understanding text and images
DeepSeek R1-Distill-Qwen-14B 14B ~12–16 GB (when quantized) Reasoning-heavy tasks when you want more capacity than smaller local models but don't want to run a much larger model
Mistral Small 3.1 24B ~12–16 GB (4-bit quantization), ~44–55 GB (unquantized) More demanding local apps, including function calling, coding, lengthy documentation, and multimodal workflows
Llama 4 Scout 109B total, 17B active ~55–80 GB High-end private LLM deployments, large-document analysis, and multimodal workloads

What you need to run an open-weight model

After choosing an open-weight model, check whether your hardware and inference can run it for daily workflows. VRAM sets the upper limit on what your GPU can handle, and quantization reduces the memory required to load the model.

The standard self-hosted LLM stack

A self-hosted LLM setup usually has five layers working together:

  • Hardware: The GPU provides the VRAM and compute power that determine which models you can run and how quickly their response times are.
  • Model: The LLM and open-weight model you choose for tasks.
  • Inference runtime: Software like Ollama or vLLM loads the model and exposes it to other applications, often through an API.
  • Retrieval layer: If the model needs private or domain-specific information, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets the system search an external knowledge source for relevant information and add that context to the model’s request before generating an answer.
  • Application layer: The chat interface, API, or workflow that sends requests to the model and uses the response.

VRAM and quantization

Model weights need VRAM while the model is loaded for inference. When the weights and runtime requirements fit in GPU memory, the GPU can perform the relevant computations without relying on slower system memory. If they don’t fit, an inference engine might offload data or compute to system memory or the CPU, which can reduce performance.

Quantization reduces the memory required by representing model weights with fewer bits. This means you can run a larger model on the same GPU. Moderate quantization can preserve most of the model’s output quality, but aggressive compression can affect complex tasks like numerical reasoning.

Self-hosting vs. cloud hosting explained

You can run an LLM locally, but that doesn’t mean you should run every request that way. Some workloads may benefit from keeping processing within your infrastructure, but others may need the scale or capabilities of a cloud provider. 

A hybrid setup lets you choose the best path for each type of request, depending on a few factors.

Privacy and compliance requirements

AI systems may process sensitive or regulated data, and your organization may have legal, contractual, or internal restrictions on where that data can be processed or transferred. For example, GDPR Chapter V sets conditions for transferring personal data to third countries or international organizations.

Running the model locally makes data residency compliance easier because you control where the processing takes place. But self-hosting doesn’t make the system automatically compliant, as you need safeguards around access, logging, and storage. Some cloud-hosted models (especially those with enterprise SLA) may have stronger access controls and other guardrails.

Cost and breakeven volume

Cloud APIs typically charge based on usage, and more tokens means a larger bill. With self-hosting, you pay for the hardware and the people operating it and spread those costs across all the requests that the system handles.

The breakeven point is where the total cost of running your own setup becomes lower than the cost of using a cloud API. If your usage is low or unpredictable, using the cloud may be more economical. But if you process a large, steady volume of requests, self-hosting may be the better choice for your organization.

💡
If you’re using LLMs for batch processing, here’s another useful tip. You can rent a GPU-powered VPS like runpod, and run it only when you need to process data. This way, you’ll ensure relative data privacy and reduce costs, since the VPS runs only when necessary.

Latency and frontier capability

A local LLM model can provide predictable latency if you have the right hardware. It also avoids the network round trip to an external provider. But local inference isn’t always faster. A large model running on constrained hardware can be much slower than an optimized cloud service. 

Cloud providers can offer highly optimized infrastructure and access to frontier models, which are the most capable models currently available for more complex reasoning tasks. If a task needs that extra capability, the frontier’s added latency may be worth sending it to a cloud model.

Here are the main differences between a self-hosted LLM and a cloud API.

Self-hosted LLM Cloud API
Privacy Greater control over where the system processes and handles data An external provider processes the data according to its service and handling terms
Cost Higher fixed infrastructure and operating costs Usage or token-based
Latency Can be predictable with enough local capacity Depends on the network, provider capacity, and rate limits
Frontier capability Limited to models you can deploy and run Easier access to the latest leading models
Maintenance Managed by internal team Mostly handled by the provider

Route between local and cloud-based LLMs in n8n

Once you’ve decided which requests run locally and which should go to the cloud, you still need a reliable way to apply rules for each one. You can hard-code that logic into individual apps, but that becomes harder to inspect and update over time as you add new models and rules.

This is where n8n comes in. n8n is a source-available automation platform where engineering teams can create AI agents and agentic workflows. You can also connect local and cloud-based models in the same workflow and use routing logic to decide which path each request takes based on workload type, complexity, or data sensitivity.

This is what a basic hybrid workflow looks like.

  • Decide what information drives the route: Use information you already have, such as a sensitivity flag, task type, request volume, or complexity score wherever possible.
  • Connect the local path: Add the Ollama Chat Model node and create an Ollama credential with your instance’s Base URL. If your workflows need an agent that can use tools, you can connect a chat model to the AI Agent node, which uses the model to decide what action to take. 
  • Add the cloud path: Add the chat model node for the cloud provider you want to use, such as the OpenAI Chat Model or Anthropic Chat Model node. This gives the workflow a second path for tasks that need to use cloud processing.
  • Choose how to route the request: Use the Model Selector node when one AI agent or chain should use different language models based on your defined rules. It checks those rules in order and supplies the first matching model to the same agent or chain. Use an If node to split the wider workflow into two separate branches, or a Switch node when you need several branches with different downstream steps.
  • Define rules: Route requests by task type, complexity, or data sensitivity. Apply data-sensitivity checks before sending the request to a cloud model. If an agent needs to inspect sensitive content to determine the appropriate route, run the inspection locally first.
  • Test both paths: Run representative local and cloud requests through the workflow and check the execution to confirm that each rule goes through the intended model. Include a sensitive test case to verify that restricted data never reaches the cloud branch.

Keep your LLM setup flexible with n8n

A hybrid setup gives you room to change your self-hosted LLM strategy as models, workflow requirements, and costs scale. Instead of committing every workload to a single environment, you can adjust the split over time depending on different requests and keep the surrounding

item.title: Why we refreshed the n8n brand
item.description: A new logo, a new typeface, and a new take on our pink, built for where n8n is going.
item.dc:creator: Jan Oberhauser
item.content:encoded:
If you have spent any time around n8n, you know how we work. We ship something, break something, learn from it, listen to what people tell us, and make it better. Then we do it again. Iteration is not a process we adopted. It is how n8n got built.

So it makes sense that we have applied exactly the same approach to our brand. On October 14, at our In The Loop conference, we introduced a new logo, a new typeface, and a refined color system, with our pink still at its center. The look is evolving. What we stand for stays the same.

Here is what is changing, why, and what is not.

First, some context

n8n is a platform where people build workflows and AI agents that connect their tools, data, and models. It started as a workflow automation tool. It is now a global community of builders working across automation and AI.

That community matters to this story. Many of you have seen our logo on things you have built, contributed to, or learned from. It is more than a shape to a lot of people, and we know that. Some of you will like the new logo right away, some will need time, and some will miss the old one. That is completely fair. I understand that, as even for me it took some time.

Why the logo changed

Our old logo was built around a simple idea: connected nodes. It represented what n8n was about. You connect one thing to another, build a workflow, and make something happen.

But look at what happens in n8n today. A person steps into a workflow and makes a decision. An agent takes an action. A model interprets information. Data moves between systems. One process triggers another. Different pieces of a system react to what is happening around them in real time. The nodes are still there, but increasingly the interesting part is what happens between them.

That is the idea behind the new logo. It is less about showing a connection and more about showing the activity that connection makes possible. It is a visual expression of n8n moving from workflows that connect things to systems that can respond, adapt, and act.

That distinction matters to us because agentic AI is not something we have bolted onto n8n. It is becoming part of how people use n8n to build. As we grow into a multi-product company, our brand needed to reflect that.

The typeface and the color

The typeface follows the same logic. n8n lives in the technical world, so the type needed to be precise. But the people using n8n are just as important as the technology: builders experimenting, solving problems, and sharing what they have made. So the typeface balances those two sides: technical without feeling sterile, precise without feeling rigid. It is the same story in a different medium.

And yes, our pink stays. It has always been part of n8n, so we have refined it and added a set of grays around it, partly to give the system more range and partly to keep it from running too wild.

What does not change

This is a zhush, not a rebuild. We did not start from scratch. We took what we had, worked out what still mattered, and built on top of it.

The things that matter most about n8n are staying exactly where they are:

  • Our community of builders, and the ecosystem we have built together
  • Connection, control, and flexibility, which is why Community Edition and model choice stay
  • The pink stays. We refined it a little, but it is still very pink
  • Who we are: curious builders who care about the people we build with, and who like to keep things a little playful

How we got here

People from across n8n worked on our rebrand; our leadership challenged it, community members saw early versions and told us what they thought. We know that is only a small slice of a community this size, and that many of you are seeing this for the first time.

See it for yourself

This is a new chapter for n8n. But it is not a departure from what came before. We are still doing what we have always done: building, learning, listening, and making n8n better. The brand refresh is another part of that process.

The new identity went live on October 14, at In The Loop. You will start seeing it across the product, the website, our community, and events. Watch the brand refresh video to see how it came together, then explore the refreshed n8n. Get all the brand details on our new brand guidelines.

And then tell us what you think, including the parts that do not work for you. That is how we have always worked: ship it, learn from it, listen, and make it better. The brand is no different. Come find us on the forum and keep shaping n8n with us.
